items.title: 3.3.3 Applications of the VSEPR model in drug designing

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.3, printed pages 58-59. Figure 3.21 (aspirin bound to COX, a published image) is not reproduced; the text carries the example.

blocks.text: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose or treat a disease. They interact with the human body at specific points, or with specific processes, called targets or substrates, through their bioactive molecules called ligands. A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand through binding; examples of targets in the body are receptors such as enzymes, proteins, nucleic acids and cellular pathways. Each drug interacts with a specific target to a different degree, a feature called the specificity of the drug or ligand.

Molecular shape is an important feature that determines how a drug interacts with a biological target: only ligands with a suitable shape can fit the active sites of a target, as a specific key fits a specific lock. The VSEPR model is successfully applied in determining the shapes of various biological systems, such as substrate recognition, ligand specificity or selectivity, and antibody recognition. For example, aspirin is an analgesic (painkiller) used as a primary medicine for relief from pain. It interacts with the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) by binding to its active site through its acetyl group, -OCCH3. The shape of the COX active site and that of the acetyl group on aspirin are compatible, so the binding succeeds and blocks COX, which is a cause of pain in the body.

blocks.alt: A green COX enzyme sits in the cell membrane with a channel leading to its active site. An arrow carries aspirin (a benzene ring with COOH and an acetyl ester group, the acetyl part in red) into the channel; the red acetyl group is shown attached to a serine (Ser) in the active site. A dashed arrow shows salicylic acid leaving. A note says the acetyl group fits the site and blocks it for good (irreversible acetylation).
